planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 3-4 inches deep in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil after the last hard frost.

directions: This Chinese species stays a tidy solitary clump rather than spreading, since it rarely produces offsets, making it a good choice for a mixed woodland bed where it won't wander. In very early spring each tuber pushes up two leaflet-divided leaves on a purple-tinged stem, followed by a compact purple-and-white striped pitcher nestled between them. Keep the planting consistently moist through the growing season and allow the soil to dry somewhat once the foliage goes dormant in summer. Because new offsets are uncommon, plan to increase your stock from seed or purchased tubers rather than relying on division alone.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

planting.note: Set tubers 3-4 inches deep in cool, humus-rich soil in early spring as the ground thaws.

directions: Ranging naturally from the Russian Far East through Korea and Japan, this is one of the cold-hardiest cobra lilies available to gardeners in northern climates. The flower stalk rises well above the trifoliate leaves, so the boldly striped spathe is easy to view without crouching down, unlike many shorter-stemmed relatives. It emerges reliably each spring in a cool, humus-rich, evenly moist woodland bed and slowly builds into a multi-stemmed clump over the years as the tubers offset. Let the soil dry somewhat after the foliage dies back in late summer to mimic its natural dormancy.

planting.note: Plant tubers in cool, well-drained, humus-rich soil in filtered shade once spring frosts have passed.

directions: Native to mountain forests of Taiwan, this species closely resembles the more familiar Arisaema consanguineum but is finer in every part, with a slimmer pseudostem and narrower, drooping leaflets arranged in an umbrella-like whorl. The narrow, elegantly striped spathe appears in spring just as the single leaf begins to unfurl above it. As a true geophyte it disappears completely by late summer, so mark its spot to avoid digging into the dormant tuber. Site it in cool, filtered shade with steady moisture during active growth and a winter mulch where temperatures dip hard.

planting.note: Plant tubers deeply, about 4-5 inches, in rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil once the soil has warmed in spring.

directions: Collected from the Himalayan foothills around Darjeeling and Sikkim, this is one of the largest cobra lilies grown in gardens, sending up a single tall stem topped by broad, three-part leaves. The strongly hooded, helmet-like spathe, ranging from green-and-white to purplish, is held at eye level in late spring and makes a dramatic specimen at the back of a shaded border. Plant it in deep, fertile, consistently moist soil and avoid waterlogging, especially during winter dormancy. Established plantings are long-lived, persisting for many years once settled into a favorable woodland site.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained woodland soil in early-to-mid spring.

directions: This Chinese woodland species carries broad trifoliate leaves above a modest spathe that reveals a distinctly swollen, bright yellow spadix tip. After pollination, the fruiting stalk elongates dramatically, carrying the ripening cluster of red berries well above the foliage for a striking late-season accent. It is a vigorous, long-lived arisaema in cultivation, slowly building into a multi-tuber clump over many years in a favorable shaded bed. Keep the soil consistently moist from spring through summer, then allow a drier dormancy once the leaves yellow in autumn.
